My dad was a teenager in the 40's on the Texas coast. When he was about 14, he somehow managed to buy a working surplus BT-13 Vultee Valiant from some old rancher that had ideas about using it for crop-dusting.

Now, dad didn't have a pilots license, but he knew better than to try and fly the thing without knowing anything about it. He went to the little airstrip outside of town and talked to the old codger that ran it. The worked out a deal where dad would work at the airport after school and on the weekends in exchange for lessons, all he had to do was pay for the fuel in the piper cub that the old man owned.

So he did this for about a year and got rated to fly. He managed to get a few hours in with his BT-13, during that time, but it used a lot more fuel than the cub did, so he was faced with the problem of not being able to afford fuel.

Now, 1943 was well past prohibition, however some counties still practiced it. Brazoria County was one of these counties. It was dry, as were a few counties around it. No one minded if you had alcohol, you just couldn't buy it. IIRC, Harris county was the closest county where it could be bought, which was about an hour away by car. Not many people were willing to drive 2 hrs round trip for a bottle of booze.

There was a fairly large sulphur industry there as well as the oil industry, and it was predominately blue collar workers and ranchers, maybe a few cotton and sugar cane farmers. These guys liked to drink.

He put two and two together and figured out how he could earn money to fuel his plane. He would go around and take orders from people. He did this after school Mon-weds. On Thursday after school he would go to the airport, hop in his plane and head to Harris county. There was a little liquor store on an old dirt road that he became a regular at. He could land on the dirt road, park the plane and go in and load up with the booze, he would fly it back and then co-opting my uncles truck, would go around and deliver it. This pretty much went on till he graduated high school in '48.

He got flight hours, fuel and a little extra pocket change, while the people in the county got somewhat legal booze.

The only real friction he had was the fact that my grandma was a devout baptist. His dad was too, but he liked to drink as well. Dad had an understanding with my grandpa that a little flask of rye whisky each week would be there is grandpa kept grandma in the dark about it all.

Now, on the other side of the family, my grandfather was the one doing it. He worked the oil fields as well, and was living in Galveston. My grandfather somehow managed to lay his hands on an old PT boat and would use it to help supply the oil fields in the gulf. I don't know the whole story, but I know that he would frequently head to Cuba on the backside of these runs and import several barrels of Rum. This was considerably more risky because he was avoiding federal taxation on booze.

TL;DR: My dad used an old army air-corps trainer to become an underage bootlegger, my grandfather on my moms side did the same only using a PT boat.
